title: Donald Trump exits the White House for the last time
description_short: Donald Trump exits the White House for the last time
description_medium: Trump left the White House on January 20, 2021, and delivered a farewell speech at Joint Base Andrews before flying to Florida. He praised his administration, said “we will be back,” and wished the incoming administration success. He did not attend Joe Biden’s inauguration, the first presidential snub of a successor’s swearing-in since 1869.
description_long: On January 20, 2021, Trump departed the White House and spoke to supporters at Joint Base Andrews before flying to Florida with Melania Trump. In his final speech as president, he called serving an honor, highlighted policies and achievements he credited to his administration, and said he expected to be “back in some form.” He also wished Joe Biden’s incoming administration “great luck and great success.” Trump did not attend Biden’s inauguration, becoming the first outgoing president since 1869 to skip his successor’s swearing-in. The departure came weeks after the January 6 attack on the Capitol; the inauguration in Washington proceeded under heavy security, with about 25,000 troops assigned to protect the ceremony. The BBC reported that Trump praised his administration’s work on jobs, the Space Force, veterans, taxes and COVID-19 vaccines, and urged caution about the pandemic. This account describes the public departure and speech; it does not treat his claims about accomplishments as independently verified.

preserved_fields.title: Donald Trump exits the White House for the last time
preserved_fields.description_short: Donald Trump exits the White House for the last time

notes: Replaced the unrelated human-rights/immigration categorization with no impact category; this entry describes a presidential departure and speech. The event details follow the linked BBC report.

title: Donald Trump never planned on winning in November
description_short: Donald Trump never planned on winning in November
description_medium: An August 2024 TrumpFile post asserted that Trump never planned to win the November election, but the record supplies no supporting quotation. A later Axios article described routine contingency planning and reported that Trump expected to win while acknowledging he could lose. That later report does not substantiate the title’s claim about his intent.
description_long: The title asserts that Trump never intended to win the November 2024 election, but the supplied TrumpFile synopsis gives no quotation or evidence supporting that conclusion. The linked TrumpFile page could not be read. A separate Axios report published on November 4 described an internal campaign email that planned for either election outcome, including winding down payroll if Trump lost and moving some staff into transition or inauguration work if he won. Axios also reported that Trump expected to win while privately acknowledging that he could lose. Contingency planning for both outcomes does not show that a campaign lacked an intention to win; the later report therefore cannot substantiate the earlier title. It also postdates the August 21 TrumpFile entry and describes a separate event. The material supports distinguishing a campaign’s routine planning from claims about a candidate’s private intent. To present the original assertion as fact, the record needs a specific contemporaneous statement or document that supports it. Until then, the claim should remain attributed as speculation or the title should be corrected.

preserved_fields.title: Donald Trump never planned on winning in November
preserved_fields.description_short: Donald Trump never planned on winning in November

notes: The TrumpFile page was inaccessible; its synopsis contains no supporting quote. The linked Axios report is dated November 4 and describes contingency planning plus Trump’s stated expectation of winning. It does not support the title’s assertion about intent. Proposed correction: provide contemporaneous evidence or retitle as an August 2024 opinion/speculation post.

title: Trump: REPORT: Trump demands fealty from national-security hires
description_short: Trump: REPORT: Trump demands fealty from national-security hires
description_medium: A report attributed to Washington Post journalists Ellen Nakashima and Warren P. Strobel said screening questions for some FBI and CIA applicants tested whether they accepted false claims about the 2020 election. The supplied account calls this a “loyalty litmus test,” but does not reproduce the questions or explain which applicants faced them.
description_long: The supplied report synopsis attributes to Washington Post journalists Ellen Nakashima and Warren P. Strobel an account of screening questions for prospective FBI and CIA hires. It says the questions tested whether candidates accepted false claims about the 2020 election and describes two sets of conspiracy claims as a “loyalty litmus test.” The account concerns hiring and screening inside national-security agencies, where political neutrality and evidence-based assessment are central to public trust. The exact wording, who administered the questions, which applicants were asked, and whether answers affected hiring decisions are not provided in the linked material available here. The NBC link concerns Trump’s desire for loyalists in a second administration but is not the Washington Post report named in the synopsis, and the TrumpFile page did not load. The claim should therefore remain attributed to the reported account rather than stated as an established government policy. The specific questions and the scope of the screening are needed to determine how broad the practice was and whether it affected agency hiring.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: REPORT: Trump demands fealty from national-security hires
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: REPORT: Trump demands fealty from national-security hires

notes: The supplied synopsis attributes the claim to Washington Post journalists but does not link their article or quote the questions. The TrumpFile and NBC pages do not establish the precise screening practice.
